title: SSE/chunking/backpressure - local repro & hypotheses (scratchpad)
content:
Purpose:
Quick personal scratchpad for the streaming-response bug we're seeing in the hosted API: intermittent long pauses between SSE/chunked frames (client sees 500-1000ms gaps instead of ~10-50ms). Collecting repro commands, logs, hypotheses and quick experiments to run locally or during a live incident.

Summary of the problem observed:
- Clients (both browser EventSource and Node fetch stream) receive bursts of tokens, then long pauses (hundreds of ms).
- Server is writing small chunks frequently (20-200 bytes, every 20-50ms) but client observes them batched.
- Appears in hosted staging and sometimes in dedicated clusters; not consistent per-request.
- Symptoms look like buffering at some intermediate layer (proxy, load balancer, TLS record coalescing, HTTP/2 flow control, or Node/Go runtime not flushing).

Repro checklist (minimal):
1) Simple Node SSE server that writes small chunks at 50ms intervals.
2) Client that measures timestamps of received chunks (print diff).
3) Test variations: direct to server, behind nginx (default conf), nginx with proxy_buffering off, and behind h2/h2c.

Server (Node/Express) quick test server (save as server.js):

const express = require('express');
const app = express();
app.get('/sse', (req, res) => {
  res.setHeader('Content-Type', 'text/event-stream');
  res.setHeader('Cache-Control', 'no-cache');
  res.setHeader('Connection', 'keep-alive');
  res.flushHeaders(); // ensure headers flushed
  let i = 0;
  const t = setInterval(() => {
    i++;
    const payload = `data: {\"i\":${i},\"ts\":${Date.now()} }\\n\\n`;
    res.write(payload); // intentionally small writes
    // Note: res.flush && res.flushHeaders vary by framework/node version
    if (i > 200) { clearInterval(t); res.end(); }
  }, 50);
});
app.listen(3000, () => console.log('sse server listening 3000'));

Client (Node) to measure arrival gaps (client.js):

const http = require('http');
http.get('http://localhost:3000/sse', (res) => {
  res.setEncoding('utf8');
  let lastTs = Date.now();
  res.on('data', (chunk) => {
    const now = Date.now();
    console.log(`${now} +${now-lastTs}ms chunk len=${chunk.length}`);
    lastTs = now;
  });
});

curl variants to use from CLI:
- curl -N http://localhost:3000/sse            # --no-buffer / --raw variations
- curl --http1.1 -N http://localhost:3000/sse # force http/1.1 to rule out http2 issues
- curl --http2-prior-knowledge -N https://localhost:8443/sse # if using https+h2

Proxy/nginx quick conf to test buffering (add to nginx.conf):
location /sse/ {
    proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:3000/;
    proxy_buffering off;          # important for SSE
    tcp_nodelay on;              # try to prevent Nagle-ish coalescing
    proxy_http_version 1.1;      # preserve chunked transfer
    chunked_transfer_encoding on;
    proxy_set_header Connection '';
}

Experiments already run and observations (timestamps are approximate):
- Direct to Node server -> client shows ~50ms gaps as expected.
- Through nginx default (proxy_buffering on) -> client sees batching: many server writes arrive in groups every ~600-900ms.
- nginx with proxy_buffering off -> mostly fixed, but still occasional 200-300ms spikes.
- Forcing HTTP/2 (curl --http2) -> more inconsistent, sometimes big pauses ~1s.
- Testing with openssl s_server (TLS) between client and server increased burstiness; suspect TLS record coalescing.

Error snippets/logs captured on client side:
- client: "received chunk after 872ms (expected ~50ms)" repeated
- Node client sometimes emits 'abort' when long pause >2s (client library timeout)

Server logs around an event (server prints i and timestamp on write):
- [ts=168_...] write i=57 ts=167...
- [ts=168_...] write i=58 ts=167...   # spaced by 50ms consistently on server

Network-level debug ideas:
- tcpdump or ngrep on loopback to see if packets are being coalesced into larger TCP segments.
- wireshark to inspect TLS records and see small writes grouped into single TLS record (and whether TLS push/padding occurs).
- strace on server to ensure write() syscalls are happening at expected intervals.

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) Reverse proxy buffering (nginx/proxy buffering on by default). Evidence: turning proxy_buffering off reduced problem severity significantly.
2) TLS record coalescing / kernel/TCP Nagle + delayed ACKs. Evidence: TLS path seemed worse; enabling tcp_nodelay and testing reduced but didn't eliminate.
3) HTTP/2 flow control settings causing the remote peer to advertise windows that cause batching. Evidence: problems reproduced with http2 in some setups/higher variance.
4) Runtime/framework flush behavior: some frameworks don't flush small writes by default unless flush() is available. Evidence: older Node versions required res.flush(); we saw differences across Node versions.
5) Load balancer (GCLB / ALB) or CDN performing proxying + buffering for bodies unless special headers present.

Quick debug steps to run during incident (ordered):
- Replicate locally with direct server/client (no proxies) -> see baseline.
- Add nginx in front with default conf -> reproduce 'batched' behavior.
- Toggle proxy_buffering off -> check improvement.
- Add tcpdump on nginx host to inspect packetization.
- Try curl --no-buffer and Node --tls-min-v1.2 variations to see TLS impact.
- Test server with http1.1 vs http2 to isolate protocol-level cause.

Minimal server-side mitigations to try:
- Ensure Transfer-Encoding: chunked and no Content-Length header.
- Set header: Cache-Control: no-transform (some proxies reencode/aggregate if they think they're allowed to).
- Add a tiny padding after every message (\n followed by long whitespace) to force flush on some proxies (hacky).
- On Node: call res.flushHeaders(); try res.flush() (connect 'compression' middleware can interfere).
- Set Connection: keep-alive + remove any header that might trigger buffering on proxies (e.g., accept-encoding?).

Client-side mitigations (temporary):
- Use curl/clients with --no-buffer / --raw flags.
- If using fetch/EventSource, measure and raise consumer timeouts and make client tolerant of bursts.
- For Node fetch, set highWaterMark smaller on stream consumer to read quicker.

Notes about HTTP/2 and multiplexing:
- HTTP/2 frames can carry DATA frames aggregated by the implementation. If the proxy's HTTP/2 stack chooses to buffer small writes to optimize frames, that will appear as batching to client.
- HTTP/2 flow control windows can cause pauses if server writes exceed window and client didn't ACK quickly.

Things to log/collect for an incident ticket:
- tcpdump pcap from client-facing LB and backend.
- server-side write timestamps (epoch ms) and syscalls trace.
- proxy/nginx config and its logs around connection.
- client-side receive timestamps with chunk lengths.
- full curl --verbose output with --no-buffer and forced protocols.

Repro commands summary (copyable):
# run server
$ node server.js

# direct client (measure)
$ node client.js

# curl no buffer (http1)
$ curl --http1.1 -N http://localhost:3000/sse

# start nginx with a conf that proxies to 3000 (default buffering ON) then run curl
$ curl --http1.1 -N http://127.0.0.1:8080/sse

# toggle proxy_buffering off and reload nginx, then re-run client

Quick TODOs for next follow-up:
- Reproduce with a minimal Go server (net/http) to see runtime differences.
- Get pcap showing TLS record boundaries when buffered vs unbuffered.
- Run same test via our hosted API front door to check if GCLB/Cloud Run is inserting buffering.
- If LB is culprit, add sniffing headers or a special endpoint that returns chunked SSE and ensure we set 'x-accel-buffering: no' or equivalent for our infra.

Random notes / pts to mention in incident blurb:
- "SSE/streaming bug: probable proxy buffering. First mitigation: disable proxy buffer for SSE endpoints. Secondary: ensure clients can use http1.1 for critical low-latency streams."
- "If we need to keep proxies for other reasons, consider aggregating tokens into slightly larger chunks server-side (e.g., send every 200ms or after N tokens) to reduce sensitivity to buffering)."

End of scratchpad. Will paste into INF-3421 ticket and attach pcaps when I have them.
